word:greek-nt:G0104.explanation: Aei means always—continually or on every occasion.

word:greek-nt:G0171.explanation: Akairōs means out of season—unseasonably or at an unsuitable time.

word:greek-nt:G0243.explanation: Allos means another or other—the one that is different from what was already mentioned.

word:greek-nt:G0294.explanation: Amphiennymi means to put on or clothe.

word:greek-nt:G0342.explanation: Renewal means the process of becoming new again or being restored to a fresh condition. It describes a real change from an earlier state, with emphasis on restored newness rather than mere continuation. This Greek New Testament word occurs twice, in Romans 12:2 and Titus 3:5. In both places, its exact force depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains renewal: a change that brings fresh life or condition.

word:greek-nt:G0500.explanation: Antichrist means an opponent of the Messiah.

word:greek-nt:G0621.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to lick.” It describes using the tongue to touch or consume something, and it expresses a specific physical action rather than a broad feeling or idea. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 16:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of licking.

word:greek-nt:G0654.explanation: Apostrephō means to turn away or to turn someone away. It can describe turning people away from wrongdoing.

word:greek-nt:G0683.explanation: Apōtheō means to push or thrust away, reject, or refuse.

word:greek-nt:G0737.explanation: This word means “now”. It points to the present time—the moment being spoken about, or the current stage of events. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 36 times across 35 verses, showing a recurring way to mark what is true or happening at the present point rather than at some distant time. Its basic force remains simple: it brings attention to the present. The surrounding verse determines whether “now” marks a present action, condition, or moment of transition.

word:greek-nt:G0768.explanation: Asher is a personal name and the name of a tribe.

word:greek-nt:G0863.explanation: Aphiemi means to permit or allow. It can also mean to leave.

word:greek-nt:G0997.explanation: Boētheō means to help or come to the rescue.

word:greek-nt:G1059.explanation: Gamaliel is a personal name, referring to a man named Gamaliel rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears twice, both times in Acts: Acts 5:34 and Acts 22:3. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what Gamaliel does or says in either passage.

word:greek-nt:G1060.explanation: Gameō means to marry, whether referring to a man or a woman.

word:greek-nt:G1165.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to disgrace” or “to expose to public disgrace.” It describes an action that puts a person openly into shame, making dishonor visible rather than keeping it private. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Colossians, so its central idea is clear even though each passage must be read in its own setting. It focuses on public exposure and the resulting loss of honor, not merely on inward embarrassment.

word:greek-nt:G1338.explanation: Diikneomai means to pass through, penetrate, or pierce.

word:greek-nt:G1367.explanation: This word means “two thousand,” expressing a quantity of 2,000. It functions as a number word, identifying how many persons, things, or beings are being counted in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 5:13. Its meaning is precise and numerical rather than symbolic by itself; the surrounding passage determines what is being counted and how the number contributes to the statement.

word:greek-nt:G1433.explanation: Dōreomai means to give or grant.

word:greek-nt:G1491.explanation: Eidos means visible form, shape, or appearance. It can describe a form like a dove, or the altered appearance of a face.

word:greek-nt:G1576.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to exclude” or “to alienate”—to shut someone out, keep someone apart, or separate them from a group or relationship. It can also describe something as being excluded. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 3:27 and Galatians 4:17. Its central idea is deliberate separation: someone is prevented from belonging, participating, or remaining connected. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G1635.explanation: Hekōn means willing, willingly, or voluntarily.

word:greek-nt:G1802.explanation: Enoch is a personal name. Scripture identifies him as Jared’s son and Methuselah’s father.

word:greek-nt:G1895.explanation: Epeidēper means since or inasmuch as.

word:greek-nt:G1918.explanation: Epigambreuo means to marry, specifically to take a deceased brother’s wife.

word:greek-nt:G1947.explanation: This word means “help”: assistance given to someone who needs support. It describes aid that enables a person to continue or accomplish what would otherwise be difficult. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:22, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word points to practical support rather than an abstract idea, and its precise force in Acts depends on the surrounding context.

word:greek-nt:G2014.explanation: Epiphainō means to appear. It can also describe light shining upon those in darkness.

word:greek-nt:G2061.explanation: Hermogenes is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Timothy 1:15, and English translations retain it as “Hermogenes.” Because it is a proper name, its ordinary function is to identify the person named; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

word:greek-nt:G2205.explanation: Zēlos means eagerness, zeal, or enthusiasm. It can also mean jealousy.

word:greek-nt:G2340.explanation: This word means “to catch,” including catching someone in a mistake or pursuing and catching something like prey. It describes the act of securing or trapping someone or something rather than merely noticing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:54, so its broader range is established by its lexical meanings rather than by many passages. The surrounding verse determines exactly how the catching or trapping is being expressed there.

word:greek-nt:G2379.explanation: Thusiasterion means an altar used for sacrifice.

word:greek-nt:G2410.explanation: Iericho is the name of Jericho, a city.

word:greek-nt:G2573.explanation: Kalōs means well or rightly. It can describe an answer or statement given correctly, as when someone answers well or says something well.

word:greek-nt:G2652.explanation: This word means “curse” or “cursed thing.” As a noun, it can name the curse itself or something regarded as cursed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 22:3. Its basic sense identifies what is under a curse or associated with a curse, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force of the term in that occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G2726.explanation: Katēpheia means gloom or dejection, a downcast expression that shows sorrow.

word:greek-nt:G2780.explanation: Kepouros means a gardener or garden-keeper.

word:greek-nt:G2825.explanation: Klinē means a bed or portable bed. It can also refer to a couch.

word:greek-nt:G2911.explanation: Kremnos means a crag or precipice. It can also mean a steep bank.

word:greek-nt:G2964.explanation: Kyroō means to ratify, confirm, or make valid. It can describe confirming love toward someone or a covenant being confirmed.

word:greek-nt:G3053.explanation: Logismos means reasoning or thinking, expressed as a thought. These thoughts may accuse or excuse one another.

word:greek-nt:G3084.explanation: Lytroō means to redeem or release by paying a ransom.

word:greek-nt:G3149.explanation: Mastos means the breast or breasts.

word:greek-nt:G3170.explanation: Megalyno means to enlarge or increase. It can also mean to magnify, as people magnify God.

word:greek-nt:G3307.explanation: Merizō means to divide into parts. It can also describe distributing something among others, as when fish are divided among people.

word:greek-nt:G3358.explanation: Metron means a measure. It can refer to a measured amount or a standard used in judging.

word:greek-nt:G3444.explanation: Morphe means form. It can also describe visible shape or outward appearance.

word:greek-nt:G3493.explanation: Nachor is the name Nahor, identified as one of the ancestors of Jesus.

word:greek-nt:G3516.explanation: Nēpios means an infant or child.

word:greek-nt:G3703.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “fruit,” referring to produce that comes from a plant or tree. As a noun, it names the tangible result yielded by growing things. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 18:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains straightforward: fruit or agricultural produce. This is a distinct Greek New Testament word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Hebrew or Greek LXX entity.

word:greek-nt:G3866.explanation: Paratheke means a deposit—something committed to a person’s care or trust.

word:greek-nt:G3912.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “be insane” or “to be out of one's mind.” It describes a person whose thinking or behavior is regarded as irrational, beyond sound judgment. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a strong description of mental or behavioral irrationality, not merely ordinary confusion or a small mistake.

word:greek-nt:G3985.explanation: Peirazo means to test or try. It can also mean to tempt, as when Jesus was tempted by the devil.

word:greek-nt:G4016.explanation: Periballō means to clothe or dress, as when a person is dressed in a garment.

word:greek-nt:G4089.explanation: This word means “bitter,” describing something sharp, unpleasant, or lacking sweetness. It can refer to a literal taste, but in James it is also used for an inward attitude marked by bitterness. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in James 3. Its basic sense remains the same whether it describes what is tasted or the harmful disposition expressed by a person. The surrounding verse determines how the word’s bitterness is being portrayed in a particular passage.

word:greek-nt:G4131.explanation: Plektēs means a striker and can also describe a violent person.

word:greek-nt:G4203.explanation: Porneuo means to commit sexual immorality or fornication.

word:greek-nt:G4449.explanation: This word means “be (fiery) red” or “to be red.” It describes something showing a red color, with the gloss suggesting a vivid or fiery shade rather than merely naming redness as an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew 16:2–3. Its normal meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what is being described as red in each occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G4470.explanation: Rhakos means a piece of cloth.

word:greek-nt:G4553.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “basket,” referring to a container used to carry or hold things. It names an ordinary physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:33, so its meaning is narrowly established by that single use and the direct gloss “basket.” The surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which the basket appears.

word:greek-nt:G4584.explanation: Semein is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or object. It is preserved as a name instead of being translated into an English concept. In the Greek New Testament, Semein occurs once, at Luke 3:26. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes the person being named, rather than describing that person’s character or role.

word:greek-nt:G4607.explanation: Sikarios means an assassin or murderer.

word:greek-nt:G4658.explanation: This word means “Scythian,” referring to a person identified as belonging to the Scythians. It functions as a people-group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 3:11. The word itself identifies a person by people-group identity; the surrounding verse determines how that designation functions in its particular statement. Its direct meaning remains the same: a Scythian person.

word:greek-nt:G4755.explanation: Strategos means a general or army leader. It can also mean a magistrate. In another use, it refers to the captain of the temple.

word:greek-nt:G5019.explanation: Tarsos means Tarsus, a city in Cilicia.

word:greek-nt:G5020.explanation: Tartaroo means to cast down to Tartarus or send to hell.

word:greek-nt:G5086.explanation: The word is the personal name “Tiberius.” It identifies a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 3:1, so its basic meaning is straightforward. As a personal name, it is not normally translated by a descriptive English word; it is carried over as “Tiberius.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the historical setting described there.

word:greek-nt:G5132.explanation: Trapeza means a table. It can refer to a table used for food or banqueting. It can also refer to a table used for money-changing or business.

word:greek-nt:G5297.explanation: Hypopherō means to bear up under, endure, or suffer.

word:greek-nt:G5363.explanation: Philanthrōpia means love of mankind or benevolence.

word:greek-nt:G5415.explanation: Fortunatus is a personal name, referring to a man named in the Greek New Testament. The name appears once, in 1 Corinthians 16:17, and is rendered “Fortunatus.” Because it is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is the identification of this individual. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain his specific role or significance in that passage.

word:greek-nt:G5482.explanation: Charax means a palisade or mound for besieging, a barricade raised against someone.

word:greek-nt:G5598.explanation: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet.

word:greek-nt:G5608.explanation: Ōneomai means to buy or purchase.
